claim: Open-source 1-6 h forecast of the chance that gusts pass a lift's wind-hold limit.
data_label: open data: MeteoSwiss SwissMetNet, 8 mountain stations, winters 2010/11-2025/26
limit: Not verified at lift towers or against real wind-hold logs; station gusts stand in for lift limits.
alt: Dark chart with two panels. Top: a held-out storm at Saentis, observed gusts rising past a 70 km/h line while a blue forecast probability made 3 hours earlier climbs ahead of them. Bottom: Brier skill against climatology by lead time, with the learned models above persistence at every lead from 1 to 6 hours.
post:
A cable car that stops for wind does not announce it. Guests find out at the top station, and the operator finds out when the anemometer crosses the limit.

I built an open-source forecaster for exactly that decision: the probability that the hourly maximum gust exceeds a chosen limit (60, 70 or 80 km/h) in each of the next 1 to 6 hours. It turns the probabilities into an operator message, guest text in German, French, Italian and English, and a JSON/MQTT feed.

I tested it on open MeteoSwiss data from 8 mountain stations, trained on winters 2010/11 to 2018/19 and scored only on the held-out winters 2022/23 to 2025/26.

At 70 km/h, averaged over the stations:
- Brier skill versus climatology: 0.41, with well-calibrated probabilities (mean calibration error 0.005).
- Versus persistence ("it is windy now, so it stays windy"): +0.13 skill.
- Storm onsets after at least 6 calm hours: 25% were warned at least 1 hour ahead, 0% for persistence. At the same operating point about a third of the warnings were false alarms.

What is not verified: these are weather-station gusts, not measurements at lift towers, and the thresholds are illustrative, not anyone's licence conditions. There is no comparison with real wind-hold logs.

If you run or plan lifts: would a calibrated 3-hour-ahead probability change how you brief guests and staff?

Code: https://github.com/Usernamepersonperson/ropeway-wind-stop-forecast
